guideTitle: 6 Best Electric Can Openers Under $20 in 2026
metaDescription: Six electric can openers, from plug-in countertop units to cordless hands-free models, compared on effort, safety and storage for tight budgets.
introParagraphs: Opening a can should not take a strong grip or a twisting wrist. An electric opener does the turning for you, and at the bottom of the price range you can choose between two very different designs: a plug-in countertop machine that cuts the rim, or a small cordless gadget that clamps onto the can and runs on its own.

That choice shapes everything else. Countertop models are sturdy and familiar but need an outlet and a permanent spot on the counter. Cordless models live in a drawer and cut along the side, which leaves a smoother lid edge, but they depend on batteries or a charge and must be seated squarely.

We evaluated six options from their specs and the strengths and weaknesses buyers describe. This guide explains what you gain at the low end of the market, what spending more would add, and which opener suits someone with weak hands, a small kitchen, or a camping bag.

products.name: Cuisinart Electric Can Opener, One-Touch, Nonslip Base
products.description:
The Cuisinart is the simplest way to open a can with almost no effort. You press one button and the machine runs the entire cut, so you never hold a lever down while the can turns. A nonslip base keeps the unit planted on the counter, and the maker positions it as one of the most practical openers for seniors.

The tradeoff is permanence. It plugs into the wall, so an outlet must be within reach, and it takes up a patch of counter space even when it is not in use. The listing does not mention a magnetic lid lifter or a detachable cutter, so cleaning and lid removal are more manual than on some rivals.

Compared with the Amazon Basics 3-in-1, it has fewer extras but a cleaner, single-purpose layout. Compared with the cordless KITCHENMUH, it does not rely on batteries. If a stable, no-fuss countertop machine is what you want, this is the safest pick.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants a one-button countertop opener with a steady base.

Nonslip base keeps the unit steady on the counter
Automatic cutting suits cans of various sizes
No lever pressure needs to be held during the cut
cons: Plug-in design needs an outlet within reach
Takes up a permanent patch of counter space

products.name: Amazon Basics 3-In-1 Electric Can Opener
products.description:
The Amazon Basics opener is three tools in one body: a can opener, a bottle opener and a knife sharpener. The stainless steel blade cuts through standard cans, an automatic stop ends the cut, and a magnetic lid holder lifts the lid away so your fingers stay off the edge. A wide, non-slip base steadies the can as it turns.

Its release and locking steps take a short time to learn, and the body is bulkier than a single-purpose opener. That bulk is the price of the extra tools.

It is more capable than the Cuisinart but needs a little more attention to operate. Against the bella it adds the magnet, which the bella listing does not mention. It suits someone who wants to clear out a drawer of separate gadgets.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a can opener, bottle opener and sharpener in one footprint.
pros: Three tools in one unit save counter clutter
Automatic stop ends the cut without watching
Magnetic lid lift keeps fingers off the edge
Wide nonslip base steadies the can while it turns
cons: Locking and release steps take a little learning

products.name: bella Electric Can Opener and Knife Sharpener
products.description:
The bella pairs a 60 watt motor with a stainless steel blade and a one-touch auto-turn feature. A removable cutting lever lets you rinse the part that touches the can, and the built-in cord storage hides the cable when it is not in use. A knife sharpener is included in the body.

The listing does not stress a bottle opener, and no magnetic lid lifter is mentioned, so you will have to pull the lid off by hand. The maximum can height is not stated either, which matters for tall cans.

It is easier to keep clean than the Cuisinart, since the cutter detaches. It also gives you a tidier counter than the Amazon Basics thanks to the cord storage. Choose it when hygiene and a neat counter matter more than a magnet.
products.bestFor: People who prioritize easy cleaning and tidy cord storage.

cons: No magnetic lid lifter is mentioned

products.name: KITCHENMUH One Touch Battery Operated Can Opener
products.description:
The KITCHENMUH is a cordless, battery-powered opener aimed at people with arthritis. One touch starts the cut with no twisting, and the listing says it works on round, square and oval cans. Stainless steel construction gives it a sturdy feel, and with no cord it stores in a drawer.

Batteries will need replacing over time, and the listing shows no battery level indicator. Weak cells can slow or stall a cut, so keep spares on hand.

Compared with the Proctor Silex, it relies on disposable cells instead of USB charging. Compared with the Cuisinart, it frees up the counter but gives up the constant power of a wall socket. Pick it when the kitchen has no spare outlet.
products.bestFor: Arthritic hands and small kitchens without a spare outlet.
pros: No cord or outlet needed, stores in a drawer
One touch starts the cut with no twisting
Listed for round, square and oval cans
Stainless steel build feels sturdy
cons: Batteries will need replacing over time
Weak cells can slow or stall a cut

products.name: Proctor Silex Hands-Free Cordless USB Rechargeable Can Opener
products.description:
The Proctor Silex is a hands-free, USB rechargeable opener that the maker says opens 60 cans on a single charge. You place it on top of the can and press the button, and it attaches itself and cuts along the side. A battery indicator shows the charge level, and the side cut leaves lid edges that you can touch.

The 60 can figure is modest, so it needs recharging more often than a larger battery would. It also has to sit squarely on the can or it will not track well.

It avoids the cost of replacement cells, which is its edge over the KITCHENMUH. It also cuts a smoother edge than the Cuisinart, which cuts the top rim. It is a good fit for picnics, camping and kitchens that do not want a wall plug.
products.bestFor: Portable use and anyone who wants smooth lid edges without buying batteries.

products.name: Muwanna Hands-Free Battery Operated Can Opener
products.description:
The Muwanna is a hands-free battery model that cuts along the side of the can and lifts the lid with a built-in magnet. One touch starts the process, and because it runs on batteries there is no cable to plug in or lose. The side cut leaves a smooth edge, so the open can is safer to handle.

The listing gives no cans-per-battery figure, so you cannot estimate running costs. The magnet works only with steel lids, not aluminum ones, which includes many pull-tab lids.

It adds a magnetic lifter that the KITCHENMUH lacks, and it uses disposable cells instead of the Proctor Silex's USB charging. It makes sense for someone who wants safe lid handling and does not mind swapping batteries.
products.bestFor: Users who want smooth edges and a lid that lifts away on its own.

buyingCriteria.explanation: This is the first fork in the road. A plug-in machine like the Cuisinart or the bella gives steady power and a fixed station, while a cordless clamp-on such as the Proctor Silex or Muwanna lives in a drawer. Countertop models need an outlet and a permanent patch of counter. Cordless models depend on batteries or charging. Pick the one that matches your kitchen layout.

Traditional openers cut the top rim, which leaves a sharp edge on the can. Side-cutting openers cut just below the rim, leaving a smoother edge that is not razor sharp. The Proctor Silex and the Muwanna are side cutters, and the Cuisinart is a standard countertop cut. If you handle open cans with bare fingers, the side cut is a clear safety advantage. A smooth edge can often be used as a cover for leftovers.

One-touch operation means you press once and the machine finishes the job. The Cuisinart, the bella and the KITCHENMUH all advertise this. The Amazon Basics adds locking and release steps that take a short time to learn. Hands that tire quickly benefit from the simplest control. Try to avoid models that require you to hold a lever down. Also consider the noise and the time the cut takes, since a slow machine that you must stand beside defeats the purpose. A model that stops by itself, as the Amazon Basics does with its automatic stop, lets you step away and stir a pot while the can finishes opening.

Battery models such as the KITCHENMUH and Muwanna need fresh cells over time, and weak cells can slow or stall a cut. USB models like the Proctor Silex remove the need for spares but need regular charging, at around 60 cans per charge. Plug-in models draw from the wall and never run out. Think about how many cans you open each week before choosing.

A magnetic lid lifter keeps fingers away from a freshly cut edge. The Amazon Basics and Muwanna list magnets, while the bella and Cuisinart do not mention one. A magnet only works with steel lids, so many aluminum pop-top lids will not respond. If you open lots of pop-top cans, do not count on the magnet. Safety is also about a stable base that does not shift mid-cut.

Food residue builds on the cutter, so removable parts help. The bella has a removable cutting lever, and its cord tucks into the body. Cordless models store in a drawer with no cable. The Amazon Basics is bulkier than a single-purpose opener. Wipe the cutter after every use to avoid buildup.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of operation
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how many steps each opener needs. The Cuisinart, bella and KITCHENMUH advertise one-touch starts, while the Amazon Basics adds locking and release steps. Models that remove the need to hold a lever scored highest for weak hands.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lid safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cut style and lid handling. The Proctor Silex and Muwanna cut along the side for smooth edges, and the Amazon Basics and Muwanna add magnets. Plain top-cutting models scored lower for finger safety.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed outlet needs against batteries and USB charging. The Cuisinart and bella need a socket, the KITCHENMUH and Muwanna need cells, and the Proctor Silex runs 60 cans per charge. Portability earned points for drawer storage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for detachable parts and tidy storage. The bella has a removable lever and cord storage, while the cordless units have no cable at all. Models with no mention of cleanup features were scored neutral.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value at this budget
howWeEvaluated.description: Lineup positioning shows the Cuisinart as the simplest countertop choice, the Amazon Basics as the multi-tool leader, and the Proctor Silex as the best cordless option. We asked whether each extra feature saves effort or just adds parts.

faq.q: Which is best for someone with arthritis?
faq.a: The KITCHENMUH and Muwanna are both designed around that need, with one-touch, hands-free starts and no cord. The Cuisinart is a good countertop alternative with a single button and a nonslip base. Whichever you choose, make sure it seats on the rim without effort. Test the release step before you rely on it, because a mechanism that needs a firm squeeze defeats the purpose of buying an electric opener. If you share the kitchen with someone who has strong hands, a countertop unit left in one spot is also easier to use than one that must be fetched from a drawer.

faq.q: What is a side-cutting can opener?
faq.a: It cuts along the side of the can just below the rim instead of the top. That leaves a smoother lid edge that is not razor sharp. The Proctor Silex and Muwanna cut this way. Many people reuse the lid as a cover for leftovers.

faq.q: Why does my cordless opener stall?
faq.a: The most common cause is a poor seat on the can rim. Weak batteries can also slow or stall the cut. Clean the cutter and reposition the opener squarely. If it still struggles, replace the cells or recharge.

faq.q: Does the magnet work on every can?
faq.a: No. A magnetic lid lifter only grips steel lids, so aluminum lids and some pull-tab lids will not respond. The Amazon Basics and Muwanna both list magnets. If you are unsure, lift the lid with a fork.

faq.q: How do I clean an electric can opener?
faq.a: Wipe the cutter after each use, because food residue builds up there. The bella has a removable lever that rinses clean at the faucet. Never immerse the motor body in water. Dry the blade to prevent rust.

faq.q: Is a plug-in or a cordless opener better?
faq.a: Plug-in models give steady power and a firm base but need an outlet and counter space. Cordless models store in a drawer but rely on batteries or charging. If you open cans daily, a plug-in is easier. Occasional users may prefer cordless.

faq.q: Do these openers fit tall cans?
faq.a: Can height limits are not stated for several of these models, including the bella. Standard soup and vegetable cans are the safe assumption, and tall cans such as large juice or pet food tins may not clear the cutter on a countertop unit. If you regularly buy oversized cans, check the product page for a height limit before ordering, and keep a manual opener as a fallback. Cordless clamp-on models are generally less sensitive to can height because they sit on top of the can instead of hanging it from a bracket.
